title: STAT 468 Final Project — Clustering Athlete Aging Curves
text:
Abstract
Athletes reach elite performance at highly variable rates. Some progress rapidly, while others develop more gradually over time. In this project, we model and cluster the rate of progression of Olympic track and field athletes using their aging curves. Unlike team sports, individual sports such as athletics allow for precise comparison through standardized scoring, as individual results are more easily measured in objective terms. To compare athletes across different event disciplines such as jumps and throws, we convert raw performances to a unified scale using the scoring system designed by World Athletics, the world governing body for athletics. 
We apply functional data analysis to smooth each athlete’s aging curve and extract dominant patterns using Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA). Because competition frequency varies by athlete and event, we address irregular and sparse observations using FPCA methods suited for unevenly spaced data.
Clustering the resulting FPCA scores percent change allows us to group athletes based on how fast they improve with age, identifying profiles such as early risers, steady performers, and late bloomers. These clusters provide both descriptive insights into developmental patterns and predictive tools for forecasting when rising athletes might reach elite standards based on early-career data.
This focus on the rate of progression enables a more adaptable and predictive framework allowing coaches, performance analysts, and high performance directors to analyze athletic development.
crumbs: STAT 468 Final Project — Clustering Athlete Aging Curves

title: 1  Question of Interest & Relevance
text:
1.1 Introduction
Athlete performance trajectories vary greatly. Some athletes achieve elite standards at a young age while others progress steadily over many years before reaching their peak. Traditional aging curve analyses often focus on the average progression or peak age. This approach obscures the diversity in how individuals develop and limits the ability of coaches, scouts, and performance analysts to tailor training and identify untapped potential.
This project addresses that gap by applying functional data analysis and clustering to classify athletes based on the rate and pattern of their performance progression. Rather than examining only final outcomes or single peak performances, the analysis will capture the complete shape of each athlete’s career trajectory from early improvement to peak and subsequent decline.

title: 1  Question of Interest & Relevance
text:
1.2 Motivation
Understanding the rate of progression provides actionable insights for:
- Coaching: tailoring training loads and peaking strategies to an athlete’s likely development path.
- Talent identification: distinguishing between “late bloomers” who may require patience and “early risers” who peak quickly.
- Long-term planning: projecting when athletes are likely to achieve qualifying standards for major competitions.
By identifying these patterns, organizations can better allocate resources, set realistic performance targets, and make informed selection decisions.

title: 1  Question of Interest & Relevance
text:
1.3 Project Objectives
The main objectives of this project are:

Develop predictive aging curves for individual athletes using observed data points fit with Sparse Functional Principal Component Analysis(FPCA).
Cluster the entire population’s aging curves into three groups based on the rate and shape of progression curve, using the percent change of their IAAF points as the measure of progression dynamics.
Classify existing athletes into meaningful development profiles by matching them to the most representative cluster. Use this classification to estimate when an athlete will achieve a world class standard and to predict their likely development path.

title: 1  Question of Interest & Relevance
text:
1.4 Planned Approach
To achieve these objectives, we will:
- Merge competition results with athlete metadata to create a longitudinal dataset for each athlete and event combination.
- Standardize performance measures (e.g., convert performance results to IAAF points) to allow cross-event comparison.
- Use refund package in R, face.sparse funcion to predict individual’s aging curves.
- Use Sparse Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) to extract dominant patterns in trajectory shapes.
- Apply k-means on sparse FPCA clustering(predicted functions) to group similar progression patterns through the whole population and 7 different event types.
- Interpret and label cluster patterns, and explore predictive assignment for athletes with incomplete career data.
This approach emphasizes progression rate and development patterns rather than absolute performance levels alone. It aims to provide a more dynamic and forward looking view of athlete development that can support practical decision making in competitive sport.

title: 2  Import
text:
2.1 Information Required
The analysis requires the following information for each athlete and event observation.
-Athlete identifier, which includes name and athlete link
-Performance, which is time for races and distance
-Event type, which comes from the event field
-Date of performance, which comes from the “date” field
-Birthdate, which comes from the “Birth.Date” field
-Athlete age at the time of performance, derived from “Birthdate” and “Date of performance”

title: 2  Import
text:
2.2 Data Sources
This project requires three datasets in total. Two datasets will be obtained from WorldAthelete.org and imported with read_csv(). These two datasets contains only the best performance per year for each athlete in each event. That means if an athlete participates in the same event multiple times in a year, only their top result is included. If the same athlete competes in multiple events in the same year, they will have one record for each event. And another iaaf-2005.json dataset is obtained from jchen1’s github and imported with read_json() .

The file career_progression.csv contains performance data, year, date, event, and athlete-link(identifiers).
The file olympics_data.csv provides athlete level metadata including name, birthdate, gender, event, game, game-link, athlete-link, nationality, and Olympic appearances(for example: performance mark and their rank)
The file iaaf-2005.json provides iaaf-points, mark and gender per event

title: 2  Import
text:
2.3 Collection Method
The two athlete related datasets have already been downloaded and imported manually using the standard read-csv() procedure. From “Birthdate” and “Performance date” we will compute the athlete age in years at the time of performance. Age is essential because aging curves are indexed by age rather than by calendar date. Additionally, the iaaf-2005.json dataset is also downloaded and imported manually. We need to convert individual athlete’s performance marks to a standard IAAF-points, so that we can compare their aging curves based on the IAAF-points across different events.

title: 2  Import
text:
2.4 Frequency of Collection
A single collection is sufficient for this study because the focus is historical performance progression. The analysis is not designed for live or streaming updates. Any future extensions that add seasons or events can append to these files and rerun the same pipeline.

title: 2  Import
text:
2.5 Assumptions and Data Preparation Notes
- Athlete age is measured in years using the difference between performance date and birthdate.
- Performance is standardized for cross event comparison using IAAF points.
- Each row in the linked dataset (linked career_progression.csv and olympics_data.csv ) represents one athlete performance on one date for one event. (details in tidy chapter)
- Athlete identifier fields must be consistent across files to enable a reliable merge.
- Basic integrity checks such as duplicate detection and valid date parsing will be performed in the tidy chapter.

title: 3  Tidy
text:
3.1 Clean Olympics_data.csv
The Olympic results file is processed to create a clean athlete-level metadata table, ensuring consistent formats, corrected anomalies, and standardized event classifications. This cleaned dataset will later be joined with career progression records to enrich performance analysis.
Key transformations:
This process produces a clean metadata table, Olympics_data_tidy
Show code
Olympics_data <- read_csv("/Users/yushiliu/Stat 468 final project/data/track and field data/olympics_data.csv", show_col_types = F) %>%
  janitor::clean_names() %>% 
  separate_wider_delim(date, delim = "–", names = c("start", "end")) %>%
  separate_wider_delim(cols = event, names = c("gender", "event"), delim = " ",
                           too_many = "merge") %>%
  filter(str_detect(event, "Wheelchair", negate = T)) %>% 
  mutate(
        # Manually fixed Aminata CAMARA's age
    birth_date = if_else(name == "Aminata CAMARA", "06 DEC 1973", birth_date),
    gender = if_else(gender == "Men's", "Men", "Women"),
    across(c(birth_date, end),  ~as.Date(format(
    as.Date(., format = "%d %b %Y"), "%Y-%m-%d"))),
    age = year(end) - year(birth_date),
         games = factor(games, ordered = T,
                        levels = c("The XXXII Olympic Games",
                                   "The XXXI Olympic Games",
                                   "The XXX Olympic Games",
                                   "The XXIX Olympic Games",
                                   "The XXVIII Olympic Games",
                                   "The XXVII Olympic Games",
                                   "The XXVI Olympic Games"
                        ),
                        labels = c("Tokyo '20", "Rio '16", "London '12", 
                                   "Beijing '08", "Athens '04", "Sydney '00",
                                   "Atlanta '96")),
    event_type = case_match(
      event,
      c("100 Metres", "200 Metres", "400 Metres", "400 Metres Hurdles", "100 Metres Hurdles", "110 Metres Hurdles") ~ "Sprints",
      c("800 Metres", "1500 Metres", "3000 Metres Steeplechase") ~ "Middle Distance",
      c("5000 Metres", "10,000 Metres") ~ "Long Distance",
      c("Heptathlon", "Decathlon") ~ "Combined Events",
      c("High Jump", "Long Jump", "Triple Jump", "Pole Vault") ~ "Jumps",
      c("Shot Put", "Discus Throw", "Hammer Throw", "Javelin Throw", "Javelin Throw (old)") ~ "Throws",
      c("10 Kilometres Race Walk", "20 Kilometres Race Walk", "50 Kilometres Race Walk", "Marathon") ~ "Road Races",
      .default = "Other"
    ),
         event_category = if_else(str_detect(event, "Metres|Walk|Wheelchair") |event %in% c("Marathon"), "Track", "Field")
         ) %>% 
  mutate(event = if_else(event == "Javelin Throw (old)", "Javelin Throw", event),
         games_year = year(end)) %>% rename("nationality" = nat)

text:
Read the raw CSV of Olympic track & field results.
clean_names() to lowercase and snake_case all column names.
Split date spans (e.g., "01 Aug 2012 – 12 Aug 2012") into start and end dates.
Split event strings into gender ("Men"/"Women") and event name, keeping remaining tokens intact.
Remove wheelchair events.
Correct one known birthdate anomaly (Aminata CAMARA).

Calculate age at Games end date.

Assign event_category as "Track" or "Field".
Normalize legacy event labels (e.g., "Javelin Throw (old)" → "Javelin Throw").
Extract games_year from the Games end date.
Rename nat to nationality.

title: 3  Tidy
text:
3.2 Clean Career_Progression.csv
The career progression dataset is cleaned to provide yearly performance records.

Key steps:

Removing duplicate rows.
Parsing competition dates.
Flagging retirement status (retired = TRUE if last competition year ≤ 2022).
Calculating training age (number of years since first recorded season) for each athlete-event.

The result is stored as Career_progression.


Show code
# load career progression data and identify athletes who are still active
Career_progression <- read_csv("../data/track and field data/career_progression (2).csv", show_col_types = F) %>% 
  distinct() |> 
  mutate(date = parse_date_time(date, orders = c("%d %b %Y", "%d-%b-%y"))) %>%
  mutate(retired = if_else(max(year) <= 2022, T, F),
         training_age = year - min(year) + 1,
         .by = c("athlete_link", "event"))

title: 3  Tidy
text:
3.3 Flatten the IAAF Reference Table (iaaf-2005.json)

Reading the JSON file containing IAAF scoring data.
Flattening the nested structure into a tidy table with columns: gender, event, mark, and points.
This creates the reference table iaaf_table.

raw_json <- read_json("../data/track and field data/iaaf-2025.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)

# Convert list of lists to a flat tibble
iaaf_table <- tibble::tibble(
  gender = sapply(raw_json, `[[`, "gender"),
  event = sapply(raw_json, `[[`, "event"),
  mark = sapply(raw_json, `[[`, "mark"),
  points = sapply(raw_json, `[[`, "points")

Standardizing event names to match IAAF vocabulary.
Converting all time-based marks to seconds (HH:MM:SS → seconds).
Adjusting women’s hurdles labels to 100mH.

The result is stored as wac_standards.

wac_standards <- tribble(

  "27:00.00", "10,000m / 10km road", "30:20.00",
  "2:06:30", "Marathon", "2:23:30",
  "8:15.00", "3000m SC", "9:18.00",
  "13.27", "110mH / 100mH", "12.73",
  "48.50", "400m H", "54.65",
  "2.33", "High Jump", "1.97",
  "5.82", "Pole Vault", "4.73",
  "8.27", "Long Jump", "6.86",
  "17.22", "Triple Jump", "14.55",
  "21.50", "Shot Put", "18.80",
  "67.50", "Discus Throw", "64.50",
  "78.20", "Hammer Throw", "74.00",
  "85.50", "Javelin Throw", "64.00",
  NA, "Heptathlon", "6500", #points 1174
  "8550", "Decathlon", NA, #1212
  "1:19:20", "20km Race Walk", "1:29:00",
  "2:28:00", "35km Race Walk", "2:48:00")

wac_standards <- wac_standards |> 
  mutate(Event = case_match(
    Event,
    "5000m / 5km road"       ~ "5000m",
    "10,000m / 10km road"    ~ "10000m",
    "110mH / 100mH"          ~ "110mH",  
    "400m H"                 ~ "400mH",
    "High Jump"              ~ "HJ",
    "Pole Vault"             ~ "PV",
    "Long Jump"              ~ "LJ",
    "Triple Jump"            ~ "TJ",
    "Shot Put"               ~ "SP",
    "Discus Throw"           ~ "DT",
    "Hammer Throw"           ~ "HT",
    "Javelin Throw"          ~ "JT",
    "20km Race Walk"         ~ "20,000mW",
    "35km Race Walk"         ~ "35,000mW",
    "Marathon"               ~ "Road Marathon",
    "Heptathlon"             ~ "Hept.",
    "Decathlon"              ~ "Dec.",
    .default = Event
  ))

#convert time to seconds
parse_mark_to_seconds <- function(mark_vec) {
  sapply(mark_vec, function(mark) {
    if (is.na(mark)) return(NA_real_)
    parts <- unlist(strsplit(mark, ":"))
    parts <- as.numeric(parts)
    if (length(parts) == 3) {
      # HH:MM:SS
      return(parts[1]*3600 + parts[2]*60 + parts[3])
    } else if (length(parts) == 2) {
      # MM:SS
      return(parts[1]*60 + parts[2])
    } else {
      # Assume plain seconds
      return(as.numeric(mark))
    }
  })
}

wac_long <- wac_standards |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Men, Women),
    names_to = "gender",
    values_to = "mark"
  ) |> 
  mutate(mark = parse_mark_to_seconds(mark), 
         gender = tolower(gender), 
         Event = case_when(
           Event == "110mH" & gender == "women" ~ "100mH",
          TRUE ~ Event))

title: 3  Tidy
text:
3.5 Summary and Importance
This unified tidy dataset forms the foundation for all subsequent modeling. By integrating performance records, event metadata, and standardized scoring into a consistent structure, it supports accurate estimation of aging curves through Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) and enables effective clustering of performance trajectories. The standardized format also ensures reproducibility and makes predictions directly interpretable across athletes, events, and time periods.

title: 4  Transform
text:
4.1 Link career progression to Olympic metadata
First we join the career progression dataset with Olympic athlete metadata (only keeping records with a known birth date), ensures unique athlete-event combinations, and keeps key identifying variables.
It then calculates:
It also removes the “h” suffix from performance to standardize hand-timed results.
Show code
athlete_bests <-
  Career_progression %>%  inner_join(
    Olympics_data %>%  filter(!is.na(birth_date)) %>%
      distinct(birth_date, athlete_links, event, event_type, .keep_all = T) %>%
      select(name, birth_date, athlete_links, event, nationality, event_type, 
             event_category, gender, games_year),
    by = c("athlete_link" = "athlete_links", "event")
  ) %>%  
  mutate(age_years = year(date) - year(birth_date), 
         age_days = as.double(
           difftime(
             date, birth_date,units = "days"
           )
         ),
         performance = str_remove_all(performance, "h")

title: 4  Transform
text:
age_years: athlete’s age in years at the time of performance
age_days: exact age in days

title: 4  Transform
section: 4.2 Classify events, compute performance_age, and convert performance to numeric marks
text:
4.2 Classify events, compute performance_age, and convert performance to numeric marks
Events are grouped into broad disciplines (e.g., Sprints, Middle Distance, Jumps) and assigned a Track or Field classification. The athlete’s age at the time of performance is calculated, and the raw performance string is converted into a numeric mark suitable for modeling.
Specifically, the code:

Assigns event_type (Sprints, Middle Distance, Long Distance, Combined Events, Jumps, Throws, Road Races, or Other) and sets event_category to either Track or Field.
Computes age_years and age_days, and removes the “h” hand-timed suffix from performance strings.
Generates mark: for Track events, parses the time string and converts it to seconds using lubridate::parse_date_time2 and difftime; for Field events, extracts a numeric distance using parse_number.



Show code
# Classify events
event_type = case_match(
      event,
      c("100 Metres", "200 Metres", "400 Metres", "400 Metres Hurdles", "100 Metres Hurdles", "110 Metres Hurdles") ~ "Sprints",
      c("800 Metres", "1500 Metres", "3000 Metres Steeplechase") ~ "Middle Distance",
      c("5000 Metres", "10,000 Metres") ~ "Long Distance",
      c("Heptathlon", "Decathlon") ~ "Combined Events",
      c("High Jump", "Long Jump", "Triple Jump", "Pole Vault") ~ "Jumps",
      c("Shot Put", "Discus Throw", "Hammer Throw", "Javelin Throw", "Javelin Throw (old)") ~ "Throws",
      c("10 Kilometres Race Walk", "20 Kilometres Race Walk", "50 Kilometres Race Walk", "Marathon") ~ "Road Races",
      .default = "Other"
    ),
         event_category = if_else(str_detect(event, "Metres|Walk|Wheelchair") |event %in% c("Marathon"), "Track", "Field")
mutate(age_years = year(date) - year(birth_date), 
         age_days = as.double(
           difftime(
             date, birth_date,units = "days"
           )
         ),
         performance = str_remove_all(performance, "h") # I will count hand timed results as legitimate
         ) %>%
    mutate(mark = if_else(
      event_category == "Track",
      as.numeric(
        difftime(
          lubridate::parse_date_time2(performance, orders = c("%H:%M:%S", "%M:%S:00", "%M:%OS", "%OS"), exact = T),
          lubridate::parse_date_time2("0", orders ="S"),
          units = "secs"
        )
      ), parse_number(performance)))

section: 4.4 Map athlete performance marks to IAAF points and join athlete_bests_clean with iaaf-table to get full dataset

title: 4  Transform
section: 4.5 Convert WAC standards to points and compute mean references
text:
4.5 Convert WAC standards to points and compute mean references
This step expresses the world-class standards on the same IAAF points scale used for athlete results. It standardizes WAC event labels and times, joins to the IAAF table using a “closest mark ≤ observed mark” rule, and fills missing scores with zero. For combined events, fixed anchors are applied (Heptathlon women = 1174, Decathlon men = 1212). Finally, it computes the mean WAC points by gender to provide simple reference lines for later visualizations.


Show code
wac_points <- wac_standards_tidy %>%
  left_join(
    iaaf_table_tidy,
    dplyr::join_by(gender, Event == event, closest(mark <= mark))
  ) %>%
  tidyr::replace_na(list(points = 0)) %>%
  mutate(points = dplyr::case_when(
    Event == "Hept." & gender == "women" ~ 1174,
    Event == "Dec."  & gender == "men"   ~ 1212,
    TRUE ~ points
  ))

mean_points_by_gender <- wac_points %>%
  group_by(gender) %>%
  summarise(mean_points = mean(points, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  tibble::deframe()

title: 4  Transform
text:
4.6 Model-preparation
This step prepares the FPCA input at the athlete–event level. It filters to records with non-missing IAAF points and age, builds a unique identifier by concatenating athlete_link and event, and selects the three fields required by face.sparse: athlete_id, performance_age (age in years at performance), and iaaf_score (IAAF points). It also creates helper vectors (id and uid) for indexing subjects during modeling.


Show code
# predict on full dataset(population)
# Filter out missing points athletes and rename for clarity
fd_data <- athlete_bests_points |> 
  filter(!is.na(points), !is.na(age_years)) |> 
  mutate(id = paste(athlete_link, event)) |> 
  select(athlete_id = id,
         performance_age = age_years,
         iaaf_score = points)

id <- fd_data$athlete_id
uid <- unique(id)

section: 4.7 Key outputs for modeling and Visualization:
text:
4.7 Key outputs for modeling and Visualization:

athlete_bests_points: season-best results with IAAF points
wac_points and mean_points_by_gender: world-class reference levels for comparison in plots

title: 6  Model
text:
6.1 Introduction
Athletic performance evolves with age, and understanding this progression is often represented as an aging curve which is of considerable interest in sports analytics. Aging curves plot an athlete’s performance level as a function of age, offering valuable insight for coaches, roster management,analysts, and player development strategies.
Traditional approaches to modeling aging curves, such as multiple regression with spline interpolation, provide limited flexibility and often fail to capture the full complexity of career trajectories. Functional Data Analysis (FDA) provides a more powerful and flexible framework for modeling aging curves by treating each athlete’s career trajectory as a continuous function over time. This approach allows for richer statistical analyses, including hypothesis testing, dimensionality reduction, and clustering. methodology is based on Functional Data Analysis in R and inspired by the paper Functional Data Analysis of Aging Curves in Sports by Alexander Wakim and Jimmy Jin (2014).
The methodology presented here is based on Functional Data Analysis with R by Crainiceanu, Goldsmith, Leroux, and Cui (2021) and is inspired by the paper Functional Data Analysis of Aging Curves in Sports by Wakim and Jin (2014). In this section, we begin with FDA fundamentals, then introduce Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) to summarize variation across curves, address sparse and irregular data via sparse FPCA, and conclude with clustering of functional data.

title: 6  Model
text:
6.2 Functional Data Analysis (FDA)
Functional Data Analysis (FDA) models an athlete’s performance over age as a smooth, continuous function called an aging curve. In practice, we only observe discrete values at certain ages, so we fit a smooth curve to these points. Formally, for athlete \(i\) at age \(t_{ij}\) we write: \[ y_{ij} = f_i(t_{ij}) + \epsilon_{ij}\]
where \(y_{ij}\) is the observed performance, \(f_i(t)\) is the smooth aging curve, and \(\epsilon_{ij}\) is the measurement error.
We approximate \(f_i(t)\) using B-spline basis functions:
\[f_i(t) \approx \sum_{k=1}^K \beta_{ik} B_k(t)\]
Here \(B_k(t)\) are spline basis functions and \(\beta_{ik}\) are coefficients that determine the curve’s shape. B-splines are piecewise polynomials joined at knots, allowing flexibility to capture complex patterns in performance trajectories.
To avoid overfitting, a roughness penalty is added:
\[
\hat{\beta}_i = \arg\min_{\beta_i} \sum_j \left( y_{ij} - \sum_{k=1}^K \beta_{ik} B_k(t_{ij}) \right)^2 + \lambda \int \left( f''_i(t) \right)^2 dt
\]
The penalty term \(\lambda \int (f''_i(t))^2 dt\) discourages excessive curvature, and \(\lambda\) is selected via generalized cross-validation (GCV).
Once fitted, we can compute the mean aging curve:
\[
\hat{\mu}(t) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N f_i(t)
\]
and the variance function:
\[
\widehat{\text{Var}}(f(t)) = \frac{1}{N-1} \sum_{i=1}^N \left( f_i(t) - \hat{\mu}(t) \right)^2
\]
Representing curves via their spline coefficients allows us to use multivariate tools like Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) to summarize patterns of variation and generate scores for visualization, comparison, and clustering.

title: 6  Model
text:
6.3 Functional Principal Component Analysis(FPCA)
Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) summarizes variation across aging curves by decomposing each curve into a mean function plus a weighted sum of functional principal components (FPCs). \[f_i​(t)=\mu(t)+\sum^K_{k = 1}\xi_{ik}\psi_k(t)\]
Here:
- \(\mu(t)\) is the mean curve
- \(\psi_k(t)\) are orthogonal basis functions (FPCs)
- \(\xi_{ik}\) are the FPC scores for athlete (i) on component (k)
The first component \(\psi_k(t)\) explains the largest proportion of variation in the data, the second explains the most variation orthogonal to the first, and so on. The scores \(\xi_{ik}\) indicate how much each athlete’s curve deviates from the mean along each component.
By retaining only the leading components that explain most of the variation, FPCA provides a compact low-dimensional representation of each curve. This allows efficient visualization, statistical testing, and clustering while preserving the main features of the original functional data.

title: 6  Model
text:
6.4 Sparse and Irregular FPCA
Sports performance data are often sparse (few observations per athlete) and irregular (different measurement ages across athletes). Traditional FDA and FPCA assume regular, dense observations, making them unsuitable for such data. In this project, many athletes have limited recorded performance points, so I use Sparse FPCA, implemented via the face.sparse() method in R. This approach follows the example from Functional Data Analysis with R (Crainiceanu et al., 2021), where sparse and irregular data are smoothed, principal components are extracted, and clustering is performed on the reconstructed curves.
Sparse FPCA can

Identify eigenfunctions that explain most of the variation in the data
Predict full aging curves even when data are sparse and irregular
Provide principal component scores for downstream analysis, such as clustering

In my project, Sparse FPCA estimates the mean function and covariance structure from incomplete data, recovers the principal component curves, and predicts scores for each athlete. This enables full-curve reconstruction and clustering of aging patterns even when the raw observations are too limited for traditional FDA or FPCA.
Here is an example of applying sparse FPCA to an athlete named Svein-inge-valvik. We first filter the dataset to remove missing values and format it so that each row contains the athlete’s ID, performance age, and IAAF score. The data is then structured into the input format required by face.sparse() which contains the observed scores y, the corresponding performance ages argvals, and a subject identifier subj.
The face.sparse() function is applied to estimate the mean aging curve, covariance function, correlation function, eigenfunctions, and eigenvalues from the sparse and irregular data. This step smooths the observed data, extracts the principal component curves, and allows us to reconstruct the athlete’s entire aging trajectory even when only a few observations are available.
For Svein-inge-valvik we use the fitted model to generate predictions of the aging curve over a grid of ages from 11 to 58 years along with 95 percent prediction intervals. The predicted curve is plotted in red with the original observed points in blue and the overall mean curve in black.
We also extract the first three eigenfunctions which represent the main modes of variation in the population’s aging curves. These eigenfunctions are key to understanding how athletes’ trajectories differ in shape such as an early peak or gradual improvement and are later used for clustering analysis.
Additionally we compute the world class standards for both men and women in the same event. This allows us to determine the performance age at which Svein-inge-valvik reaches world class performance providing a meaningful benchmark in the context of elite athletics.
Codes are here:


Show code
# Filter out missing points athletes and rename for clarity
fd_data <- athlete_bests_points |> 
  filter(!is.na(points), !is.na(age_years)) |> 
  mutate(id = paste(athlete_link, event)) |> 
  select(athlete_id = id,
         performance_age = age_years,
         iaaf_score = points)
fd_data_shiny <- athlete_bests_points |> 
  filter(!is.na(points), !is.na(age_years))

#use face to conduct sparse FDA
top_10_ids <- fd_data |>
  count(athlete_id, sort = TRUE) |>
slice_head(n = 10) |>
 pull(athlete_id)

fd_data_top10 <- fd_data |>
  filter(athlete_id %in% top_10_ids)

id <- fd_data_top10$athlete_id
uid <- unique(id)
face_input <- data.frame(
  y = fd_data_top10$iaaf_score,
  argvals = fd_data_top10$performance_age,
  subj = id)

Sample <- which(uid == "https://worldathletics.org/athletes/norway/svein-inge-valvik-014215542 DT")

fit_face <- face.sparse(face_input, argvals.new = seq(11, 58, by = 1))
#create a data double
data.h <- face_input
tnew <- fit_face$argvals.new
#prepare data for prediction
seq <- seq(11, 58, by = 1)
k <- length(seq)
for(i in Sample){
  sel <- which(id == uid[i])
  #dati <- fd_data_top10[sel,] 
  

dati <- fd_data_top10[sel, ] |> 
  dplyr::transmute(y = iaaf_score,
         argvals = performance_age,
         subj = athlete_id)

# Create the prediction dataframe
dati_pred <- data.frame(
  y       = rep(NA, nrow(dati) + k),
  argvals = c(rep(NA, nrow(dati)), seq),
  subj    = rep(dati$subj[1], nrow(dati) + k)
)

dati_pred[1:nrow(dati), ] <- dati

yhat <- predict(fit_face, dati_pred)


Ord  <- (nrow(dati) + 1):(nrow(dati) + k)

#Plot
plot(dati$argvals, dati$y,
     xlab = "Performance Age (years)",
     ylab = "IAAF score",
     pch = 19, col = "blue",
     xlim = range(seq),
     ylim = range(c(dati$y, yhat$y.pred[Ord]), na.rm = TRUE),
     bty = "n")

lines(seq, yhat$y.pred[Ord], col = "red",  lwd = 2)
lines(seq, yhat$y.pred[Ord] + 1.96 * yhat$se.pred[Ord], col = "red", lty = 2)
lines(seq, yhat$y.pred[Ord] - 1.96 * yhat$se.pred[Ord], col = "red", lty = 2)
lines(seq, fit_face$mu.new, col = "black", lwd = 2)

}

#extract mean, covariance, variance, correlation function, and eigenfunctions
#Smooth marginal mean
m <- fit_face$mu.new
#Smooth covariance
Cov <- fit_face$Chat.new
#Pointwise covariance
Cov_diag <- diag(Cov)
#Smooth correlation 
Cor <- fit_face$Cor.new
#Pointwise prediction intervals
m_p_2sd <- m + 2 * sqrt(Cov_diag)
m_m_2sd <- m - 2 * sqrt(Cov_diag)
#Smooth eigenfunctions 
eigenf <- fit_face$eigenfunctions
#Smooth eigenvalues 
eigenv <- fit_face$eigenvalues

#first 3 eigenfunctions
par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 0, 2))
col_me <- c("cornflowerblue", "aquamarine3", "coral1")

plot(1, type = "n", xlab = "Performance Age (years)", ylab = "",
     xlim = range(tnew), ylim = range(eigenf), bty = "n")

for(i in 1:3){
  lines(tnew, eigenf[,i], col = col_me[i], lwd = 3)
}

legend("topright", c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3"), 
       col = col_me, lty = 1, bty = "n", lwd = 3)

title: 6  Model
text:
6.5 Clustering on FPCA predictive function
Clustering of FPCA groups athletes with similar aging curve shapes into distinct categories. In this project, the clustering is based on the percent change of the IAAF-points of their aging curves, which reflects the relative progression of performance over time rather than absolute performance levels. After applying sparse FPCA, each percent change curve is summarized by a small set of principal component scores, reducing the infinite-dimensional curve to a low-dimensional representation. These score vectors are then clustered using k-means, with the number of clusters set to three. This method partitions the population into distinct aging patterns, such as early peak, late peak, or sustained performance, enabling clearer comparisons between athletes with similar career trajectories. After clustering the entire population’s performance trajectories, we can assign new athlete to an existing cluster. This allows us to immediately place the athlete within a known progression pattern and monitor their trajectory over time.
Here is code for clustering the whole population based on the athletes’ percent change of IAAF-points.


Show code
#cluster the whole population based on percent change
# set up
id <- fd_data$athlete_id
uid <- unique(id)
#set the grid where to predict
seq <- seq(11, 58, by = 1)
k <- length(seq)
n <- length(uid)
# Set the predicted percent change in IAAF points matrix: one fewer column since we lose first value
PercentChange_mat <- matrix(NA, nrow = n, ncol = k - 1)

# loop over each athlete, predict every curve
for(i in 1:n){
  sel <- which(id == uid[i])
  dati <- fd_data[sel, ] |>
    mutate(y = iaaf_score,
              argvals = performance_age,
              subj = athlete_id) |> 
    select(y, argvals,subj)
 
#if (nrow(dati) == 0) next
  
dati_pred <- data.frame(y = rep(NA, nrow(dati) + k),
                          argvals = c(rep(NA, nrow(dati)), seq),
                          subj = rep(dati$subj[1], nrow(dati) + k)
  )
  
  dati_pred[1:nrow(dati), ] <- dati
  yhat <- predict(fit_face, dati_pred)
#Extract just the predictions on the grid  
  Ord <- (nrow(dati) + 1):(nrow(dati) + k)
  raw <- yhat$y.pred[Ord]

# Check if prediction is valid
if (all(is.na(raw)) || any(raw[-1] == 0, na.rm = TRUE)) next

# Compute percent change: (current - previous)/previous * 100
pc <- c(NA, diff(raw) / head(raw, -1)) * 100

# Save to matrix, dropping the initial NA
PercentChange_mat[i, ] <- pc[-1]
}

# conduct clustering of predicted functions from fpca sparse(k-means clustering)
set.seed(20240805)
cl_kmeans <- kmeans(PercentChange_mat, centers = 3, nstart = 25)
cl_ind <- cl_kmeans$cluster
cl_cen <- cl_kmeans$centers

# plot the predicted aging curves together with the estimated clustering as well as centers of the clusters
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
colset <- c("#E69A8DFF", "#F6D55C", "#2A9D8F", "#5F4B8BFF")
plot(NULL, xlim = range(seq), ylim = c(-20, 20),
     xlab = "Performance Age (years)", ylab = "Percent Change in IAAF Score", bty = "n")

for(i in 1:n){
  lines(seq[-1], PercentChange_mat[i,], col = colset[cl_ind[i]])
}

for(j in 1:3){
  lines(seq[-1], cl_cen[j,], col = "black", lwd = 3)
}
legend("topright", legend = paste("Cluster", 1:3),
       col = colset, lty = 1, lwd = 2, bty = "n")

Here is an example of an aging curve for a sample athlete. This athlete(Aadam-ismaeel-khamis) can be assigned to one of the existing clusters, which allows us to predict and monitor the athlete’s performance trajectory over time. This athlete’s predicted aging curves is very align with the third cluster above(green cluster), so we can interpret this athlete as early risers.

I also cluster the entire population by event type to compare patterns across different disciplines. The population is divided into seven event types: Sprints, Middle Distance, Long Distance, Combined Events, Jumps, Throws, and Road Races. For most event types, the resulting clusters are similar to those of the overall population, while a few categories such as Middle Distance and Road Races show noticeable differences.

title: 7  Communicate
text:
7.1 Delivery Format
The findings from this analysis will be delivered through an interactive Shiny dashboard, which integrates:

title: 7  Communicate
text:
Dynamic aging curve exploration for individual athletes and population-level trends
Trelliscope panel plots for side-by-side comparison across multiple athletes and events

title: 7  Communicate
text:
7.2 Overview
The final insights will be provided to key stakeholders, including coaches, performance analysts, sports scientists, and sports development directors. The Shiny dashboard will serve as a centralized platform for exploring aging curves, identifying cluster patterns, and comparing event-specific performance trends.
Because aging curves evolve over time and are tied to an athlete’s age, the dashboard will be updated annually to maintain accuracy and relevance. This will allow stakeholders to track changes in trajectories, compare against historical benchmarks, and adjust training or selection strategies accordingly.
By providing accessible, data-driven insights, the dashboard will support evidence-based decision-making in training program design, athlete selection, and long-term talent development planning.

title: 7  Communicate
text:
7.3 Clusters interpretation
Three primary aging curve patterns are identified through clustering:

Early risers: Rapid gains early in a career, reaching a plateau sooner
Steady performers: Consistent year-over-year improvements, leading to a smooth peak
Late bloomers: Gradual early progress followed by substantial improvement later in the career

When clustering is performed by event type, most disciplines show patterns similar to the overall population clusters. However, certain events, such as Middle Distance and Road Races, display noticeably different cluster structures.

title: 7  Communicate
text:
7.4 Application Example:
A new athlete’s aging curve can be predicted using the face.sparse method and matched to one of the existing clusters. This allows stakeholders to immediately identify the athlete’s most likely performance trajectory and monitor changes over time.
The following plot has observed data points in black, and predicted aging curves in blue curve, and also a red dashed line interprets world class standards for men(1147.174) . The athlete is called “abdi-abdirahman”, and he attends 10000m event. We classify this event to event type(Long Distance), and compare his aging curves to the clustering plot, we can assign him to the third cluster (green).

title: 7  Communicate
text:
7.5 Key insights for Stakeholders
Performance evolves with age: Although the population mean curve shows the general trend, each athlete’s performance path is unique. Principal components highlight these differences, revealing whether an athlete peaks early, improves steadily, or peaks later in their career.
Cluster shapes are actionable: Knowing whether an athlete is an early improver, steady performer, or late bloomer can guide training focus and competition scheduling.
World Athlete Championships (WAC) context is informative: Comparing an athlete’s performance to world-class benchmarks (WAC mean) helps put their achievements into perspective across different ages and events.

title: 7  Communicate
text:
7.6 Limitations and Considerations
Data sparsity: Predictions depend on smoothing methods. Athletes with very limited career data will have wider uncertainty bands around their estimated curves.
Join granularity: Scoring uses a “closest less-than-or-equal-to” rule for matching performances to reference tables. For athletes whose results are close to table knots, small shifts can occur in assigned point values.
Causality: Aging curves describe associations between performance and age. They do not imply causal effects of age, training, or other factors on performance changes.

title: 7  Communicate
text:
7.7 Next steps
Event-type stratification: Fit separate FACE models for each event type (for example, sprints, middle distance, throws) and compare their mean aging curves to determine whether different disciplines follow distinct performance trajectories.
Uncertainty visualization: Incorporate visualizations of individual confidence intervals within the Shiny dashboard’s comparison view so that coaches can weigh the reliability of predicted trajectories.
Trajectory monitoring: Implement year-over-year tracking of within-athlete shifts in curve shape (for example, an early peak evolving into a stable phase) and generate alerts when an athlete moves to a different cluster.
Robust clustering: Evaluate robust clustering methods such as trimmed k-means to improve stability in the presence of outliers, and refine the number of clusters using within-cluster sum of squares (SSE) methods as described in the reference paper.
Selection bias adjustment: Address potential right-tail selection bias, as higher-performing athletes tend to remain in competition longer, which may skew the observed distribution of aging curves.
